edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: Ukraine’s air-defence needs, a record crypto theft and a Danish arms-funding scandal lead the morning’s coverage, alongside political and public-service developments across the UK and Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises fresh developments and consequential reporting. Returning stories are included only where the gather adds a material update or distinct reporting dimension; unresolved claims and legal proceedings remain attributed.

content.headline: US approves 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine, but delivery may take years
content.shortHeadline: US approves 500 Patriots for Ukraine, but delivery may take years
content.standfirst: The $2.1bn sale will be paid for by Kyiv’s allies, but Ukraine says it needs interceptors now as Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure intensify.

image.caption: Volodymyr Zelenskyy stands beside a Patriot air-defence system in Germany in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years

segments.body: The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for $2.1bn. The State Department says Canada, Germany and Norway will fund the purchase, alongside Ukrainian national funds financed through an EU support loan. Zelensky welcomed the decision but said the missiles are needed now to counter Russian attacks.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that the missiles have yet to be manufactured and may not arrive until the early 2030s. Zelensky has urged allies to provide missiles from existing stockpiles while new production catches up.

segments.body: The delivery schedule has not been announced. The BBC reports that the order is understood to be for newly built missiles, with production capacity limited; Ukraine says Russia has stepped up attacks on energy infrastructure ahead of winter. The purchase follows a period of tension between Kyiv and Washington over military support and policy towards Russia.

content.headline: Binance races to recover $6.3bn in crypto theft linked by analysts to North Kore
content.shortHeadline: Binance tries to recover $6.3bn in record crypto theft
content.standfirst: The world’s largest crypto exchange says it has frozen or secured some of the stolen assets and will cover customer losses. Analysts suspect a North Korean hacking unit, but the breach and recovery remain under investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’
How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?
Verdenshistoriens dyreste bankrøveri skete på 20 minutter og kan trække tråde til Nordkorea

segments.body: Binance says hackers accessed about $6.3bn in digital assets in a record crypto theft. The exchange says it has secured around half the funds and set aside more than $6.34bn to cover the loss. Several analytics firms have linked the attack to a North Korean hacking unit; that attribution has not been established by a court.

perspectives.body: The Guardian notes that crypto customers generally lack the deposit protections available to bank customers. Binance’s promise to cover losses comes from the company itself, rather than a government-backed guarantee.

segments.body: Binance initially suspected an engineer’s laptop was compromised, then said investigators found additional points of breach. The US Secret Service and FBI are assisting. The exchange says customer funds are safe, but experts caution that customers’ options if Binance fails to honour its promise would depend on their contracts and where the company could be sued.

content.headline: Polish government and top court clash as police enter court grounds
content.shortHeadline: Poland’s court crisis escalates as police enter tribunal grounds
content.standfirst: The confrontation between Donald Tusk’s government and the Constitutional Court has intensified after senior justices were suspended and prosecutors sought to lift their immunity. Both sides dispute the legality of the moves.

image.caption: Police officers outside Poland’s Constitutional Court in Warsaw during the dispute over the court’s leadership.

sources.originalTitle: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
Præsident for forfatningsdomstol i Polen suspenderet

segments.body: Riot police were deployed at Poland’s Constitutional Court in Warsaw amid a stand-off with the government. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has sought to lift the immunity of court president Bogdan Święczkowski and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański so criminal charges can be brought against them. President Karol Nawrocki, backed by the opposition Law and Justice party, interrupted a trip to attend the confrontation.

perspectives.body: DR’s account says the court has described the events as a coup and reports that President Nawrocki has refused to swear in judges elected by parliament. It also says the court’s president disputes that the judges chosen by the parliamentary majority can take up their duties.

segments.body: Tusk says restoring the rule of law requires decisive action. The dispute builds on years of conflict over judicial appointments: European courts previously ruled that the Constitutional Court was no longer an independent and impartial tribunal. Critics of the government’s current actions warn that removing the court’s leadership by executive action could also damage the rule of law.

content.headline: G20 foreign ministers’ group photo cancelled after protests over Russia
content.shortHeadline: G20 photo scrapped after countries refuse to appear with Russia
content.standfirst: The US cancelled the customary group photograph in Atlanta after several delegations said they would not stand alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. The dispute reflects wider divisions over Ukraine and Russia’s place in international forums.

image.caption: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta.

sources.originalTitle: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia

segments.body: The traditional G20 foreign ministers’ “family photo” was cancelled after the UK, Australia and European delegations objected to appearing with Russia’s Sergei Lavrov. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the hosts chose to avoid turning a ceremonial event into a distraction from the meeting’s work.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that about a third of delegations signalled they would not take part in a joint photograph with Russian representatives. Australia said it would not normalise Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

segments.body: UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused Russia of killing civilians in Ukraine and called for pressure to secure a just peace. Ukraine was not invited to the meeting. The participants’ divisions over the war and other issues may also prevent them agreeing a joint statement.

content.headline: Global nature talks agree action plan, but funding gap remains
content.shortHeadline: Nature talks reach deal, but funding still falls short
content.standfirst: Countries meeting in Armenia agreed key parts of a plan to get the world’s biodiversity targets back on track. Progress remains far behind the 2030 goals, with governments and companies yet to provide the funding needed.

image.caption: Elephants in southern Africa, among species cited as recovering through conservation efforts.

sources.originalTitle: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

segments.body: Delegates from nearly 200 countries agreed key parts of an action plan at the UN nature talks in Yerevan, after negotiations ran past their scheduled end. The agreement recognises that countries are falling behind commitments made in 2022 to halt and reverse nature loss; the UN says the world is on track to meet only one of the 24 targets.

segments.title: Money and implementation
segments.body: More than $1bn was pledged at the meeting, including half from philanthropists, but funding remains a major obstacle. The 2022 agreement set a $30bn public funding goal by 2030 and called for a further $170bn from private sources. The talks also exposed disputes over harmful subsidies and the voluntary contributions expected from companies that profit from genetic material.

content.headline: Hundreds leave occupied Oleshky in rare Ukraine ceasefire operation
content.shortHeadline: Hundreds evacuated from Oleshky during rare Ukraine truce
content.standfirst: A short ceasefire window enabled residents to leave the Russian-held city in southern Ukraine, while several hundred others stayed amid severe shortages. The truce is due to last until Sunday; its wider implications remain uncertain.

image.caption: Residents gather in Oleshky before the evacuation convoy set off through Russia and Belarus.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky

segments.body: Hundreds of people were evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during a four-hour window on Friday, in a joint operation organised under a local ceasefire. A convoy of 25 buses and ambulances helped residents leave; they are travelling through Russian-held territory and Belarus before reaching Ukraine-controlled territory.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that residents have faced serious food and medical shortages, and that some who remained have survived on very little. It also cites a volunteer who says Russian troops are checking empty homes and, in some cases, moving into them.

segments.body: Several hundred residents chose to stay. Ukrainian authorities say aid will be arranged for them, while Russia says it has prepared supplies. The ceasefire is due to end on 1 November. Residents elsewhere in the Kherson region fear Russia may use the pause to reinforce its positions; Moscow has said the local arrangement should not be read as a willingness to extend a truce across Ukraine.

content.headline: Thai lawyer receives 34-year sentence total under monarchy insult law
content.shortHeadline: Thai lawyer’s sentences under royal insult law exceed 34 years
content.standfirst: Arnon Nampa was given another prison sentence for a speech calling for scrutiny of Thailand’s monarchy. He faces 14 cases under the law, with two verdicts still pending, as rights advocates warn it has chilled public debate.

image.caption: Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at a protest in Bangkok in 2020.

sources.originalTitle: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years

segments.body: A Bangkok court sentenced human rights lawyer Arnon Nampa to two years and eight months for violating Thailand’s lèse-majesté law. The sentence brings the total he has received across 14 cases to more than 34 years; verdicts in two cases are still pending. Nampa has been in prison for three years and has seen his young children only during court hearings.

segments.title: A law with a broad reach
segments.body: The BBC reports that 294 people, including 20 under 18, have been prosecuted under the law since 2020, with sentences of up to 50 years. A lawyer who works with defendants says the terms “defame” and “insult” are interpreted so broadly that even questioning the law can lead to prosecution. Thai officials say the measure reflects the country’s culture and history.

content.headline: Burnham open to formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade, rejects repar
content.shortHeadline: Burnham open to slavery apology, but rejects reparations
content.standfirst: Ahead of the Commonwealth summit, the prime minister says he is willing to discuss a formal state apology and proposes restructuring debt for poorer member states. Caribbean leaders welcome the opening but say financial reparations must remain part of the conversation.

image.caption: Andy Burnham said he wanted to express sorrow and regret for the suffering caused by the slave trade.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade

segments.body: Andy Burnham says he is open to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state for the transatlantic slave trade and offers structured talks with affected countries and campaigners. He expressed personal sorrow and regret for the suffering caused, but said financial reparations are not the right answer.

segments.title: Different views on what dialogue means
segments.body: Burnham proposes a drive to restructure debt for the poorest Commonwealth countries, led by former prime minister Gordon Brown. Caribbean leaders cautiously welcomed the offer of dialogue and debt relief, but several said an apology without discussion of reparations would be insufficient. The Commonwealth summit begins on 1 November.

perspectives.body: Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley welcomed Burnham’s move while making clear that their positions on reparations differ. Antigua and Barbuda and Jamaica also welcomed the offer of dialogue, while insisting their reparatory-justice claims remain.

content.headline: Police Scotland makes early inquiries into Epstein and Andrew’s Balmoral visits
content.shortHeadline: Police Scotland opens early inquiries into Balmoral visits
content.standfirst: The force says it has received information and is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell at Balmoral. The allegations are not findings of wrongdoing, and the inquiry is at an early stage.

image.caption: An image released during Ghislaine Maxwell’s trial appears to show her and Jeffrey Epstein at Balmoral.

sources.originalTitle: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
The photos and flight logs that shed light on Andrew and Epstein’s Balmoral trip

segments.body: Police Scotland says it is making active inquiries into information about visits to Balmoral by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. The Daily Express reported that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence; police have not confirmed details and say the work is at a very early stage.

A photograph released during Maxwell’s trial appears to show her and Epstein at Balmoral in 1999. Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein. Police say their inquiries are evidence-led and that the needs of survivors are central.

perspectives.body: The i Paper adds that the reported inquiry comes amid other UK police reviews of information in the Epstein files, including claims concerning flights and alleged trafficking. It reports no finding that the claims about Balmoral are proven.

content.headline: Poundland rescue bid rejected as administration and store closures loom
content.shortHeadline: Poundland rescue bid rejected as store closures loom
content.standfirst: The retailer’s US owner has rejected a management-backed offer for the whole chain, which has sought temporary protection from creditors. Suppliers are holding back deliveries as a search for a buyer or break-up proceeds, putting jobs at risk before Christmas.

sources.originalTitle: Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed

segments.body: Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving it 10 days’ protection from creditor demands while a solution is sought. Its owner, restructuring firm Gordon Brothers, rejected a management-backed bid for the entire chain from Martin Property Group. Suppliers are holding back deliveries, and the retailer operates about 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland.

segments.title: A pressured business model
segments.body: Poundland has struggled with higher costs and crowded competition in the discount market. It has widened its range beyond £1, while sales and profits have fallen. The owner is understood to be considering offers for parts of the business; Andy Burnham has called for the reasons for rejecting a rescue bid to be explained. Gordon Brothers did not comment on claims about fees and interest taken from the chain.

content.headline: More than 200 residents leave east London flats over possible structural colla
content.shortHeadline: East London residents evacuated over tower block collapse risk
content.standfirst: Residents of three Canning Town apartment blocks were ordered out after engineers identified cracks and sagging in structural slabs. They have not been told when it will be safe to return or who will cover longer-term costs.

image.caption: The Canning Town apartment development where residents were evacuated over structural concerns.

sources.originalTitle: I had to flee my £335,000 new-build flat over risk of tower block collapse

segments.body: Residents in more than 200 apartments across three blocks in Canning Town were told to leave at about 2am on Saturday because of “serious structural issues” that could pose a risk to life. The buildings, part of the Royal Gateway development, are less than 10 years old. Some residents say they have found temporary accommodation with family or friends.

The property manager says cracks and sagging in transfer slabs beneath the blocks prompted the evacuation and that safety is its immediate priority. Newham Council says it opened a rest centre and provided emergency accommodation on the night. Residents say they have not received clear information about longer-term housing or reimbursement.

content.headline: Russell Brand trial: prosecutor says accusers had ‘nothing to gain’
content.shortHeadline: Brand trial hears prosecution’s closing case from six women
content.standfirst: The prosecutor says six women came forward with no appetite for publicity and describes their accounts to jurors. Brand denies seven charges, including rape and sexual assault; his defence is due to make its closing speech on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand trial: accusers have ‘nothing to gain’ and were not led by media, court told

segments.body: In closing arguments at Southwark Crown Court, prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors that six women had “nothing to gain” by giving evidence against Russell Brand and had come forward after realising they were not alone. She said their accounts described a similar pattern of behaviour. These are the prosecution’s arguments, not findings by the jury.

Brand, 51, denies seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, relating to six women and allegations spanning 1999 to 2009. His barrister is due to deliver the defence closing speech on Monday. The jury will consider the rival arguments before reaching verdicts.

content.headline: UK trial tests whether breast cancer radiotherapy can be shortened to five days
content.shortHeadline: Trial tests five-day radiotherapy for early breast cancer
content.standfirst: More than 1,000 people have joined a UK study testing a five-day treatment course instead of three weeks. Researchers hope it will reduce hospital visits and side effects, but results are not expected until 2033.

image.caption: A UK trial is testing a shorter radiotherapy course for early-stage breast cancer.

sources.originalTitle: The radical new breast cancer trials to cut gruelling radiotherapy sessions by two-thirds

segments.body: The FAST-Forward Boost trial is testing whether radiotherapy for early-stage breast cancer can be delivered over five days rather than three weeks, with an additional targeted dose. It is running at 39 UK hospitals and aims to recruit more than 4,000 participants, who will be followed for five years.

Researchers hope fewer treatment visits could reduce the burden on patients and families and free NHS capacity. The approach is being tested, not established as a replacement for current treatment; results are expected in 2033. The study is led by the Institute of Cancer Research and funded through the National Institute for Health and Care Research.

content.headline: Medical micro-robots show promise for targeted drug delivery and treatment
content.shortHeadline: Tiny medical robots could deliver drugs more precisely
content.standfirst: Researchers are developing magnetically guided devices to deliver drugs in the gut and, in early tests, through blood vessels. The technologies remain experimental; several are years from possible use in patients.

image.caption: Illustration of a medical micro-robot designed to deliver drugs to a precise location in the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: A swallowable capsule camera is already used in the NHS to investigate gut problems. More experimental devices aim to go further: a 6.5mm magnetic robot delivered insulin to the lower intestine of pigs in a study, while another 2mm device has been guided through a pig’s bloodstream in testing.

Researchers say precise delivery could allow smaller drug doses and potentially help treat tumours, infections or blood clots. Some proposed approaches have so far been demonstrated only in animals or models; experts say devices small enough to travel through human blood vessels may be at least a decade from patient use.

content.headline: Danish parties demand answers over 71m kroner lost in Ukraine ammunition deal
content.shortHeadline: Danish MPs demand answers over €71m Ukraine ammunition deal
content.standfirst: Denmark’s donation to Ukraine was channelled through Estonia to a company that delivered no ammunition, and Danish defence spokespeople say they were not informed of the months-old Estonian scandal. The minister says most of the money is being returned.

sources.originalTitle: Skandalesag om fup-selskab var kendt i månedsvis, men forligskreds fik intet at vide
Falsk våbenfirma brugte AI-billede og fik 71 millioner – det vil ske igen, mener eksperter

segments.body: Denmark gave Estonia 71 million kroner for ammunition for Ukraine. Estonia’s defence investment centre paid the money to Datasel, an Italian-Indian company that did not deliver ammunition. The company is now in a legal dispute with Estonia. Danish defence spokespeople say they were not told about the case, which had been a scandal in Estonia for months.

perspectives.body: TV 2 reports that Datasel’s website used AI-generated tank imagery and a picture taken from a video game. Two defence experts say urgent weapons buying increases the risk of mistakes and fraud, though they disagree about whether the overall risk is acceptable.

segments.body: Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus says Estonia has agreed to return the donation regardless of the court case, and that most of the money is already on its way back. Opposition parties want an account of why the Danish parliamentary defence committee was not informed. The gather does not establish why Estonia selected Datasel or whether the funds will all be recovered.

content.headline: AI-generated access requests target at least 50 Danish education institutions
content.shortHeadline: AI bot sends mass information requests to Danish schools
content.standfirst: At least 50 education institutions have received rapid-fire requests about their systems and legal cases. The ministry says it believes an AI bot sent them and reports no indication that data has been compromised; schools remain alert to possible cyber risks.

image.caption: Frederiksberg Gymnasium, one of the schools that received suspicious information requests.

sources.originalTitle: 'Det er så mærkeligt': Danske skoler ramt af mystiske AI-anmodninger

segments.body: At least 50 Danish education institutions have received large numbers of access-to-information requests from the same sender, the Education Ministry says. Frederiksberg Gymnasium’s rector says the requests sought information about school systems and court cases, and follow cyberattacks on some education institutions. The ministry assesses the sender to be an AI bot.

School leaders fear the requests could be an attempt to learn how to access sensitive personal data, but the ministry says it has no current indication that data has been compromised and is monitoring the situation with relevant authorities. Schools are legally required to process access requests promptly, leaving institutions to assess how to handle suspicious ones.

content.headline: Danish authorities pursue Arizona property in tax-dividend fraud case
content.shortHeadline: Denmark pursues US properties in tax-fraud recovery case
content.standfirst: Danish tax authorities allege that an Arizona property company received proceeds from the dividend-tax fraud and used them to buy real estate. The company denies knowingly handling fraud proceeds; the Dubai court case is ongoing.

image.caption: Cigarette packs marketed on Emerald Industries’ website; DR says it could not identify a retailer for the products.

sources.originalTitle: Afsløring: Dansk milliardjagt fører til mystisk amerikansk cigaretfirma

segments.body: Danish authorities are seeking control of, or compensation for, Arizona properties they say were bought with money from the dividend-tax fraud associated with Sanjay Shah. Court documents cited by DR say the claim against Emerald Industries is worth more than $22m, with a lower alternative claim if the main demand fails.

segments.title: What remains disputed
segments.body: Emerald categorically denies knowingly receiving or handling proceeds from fraud and says payments were for legitimate cigarette business. DR found limited public information about the company’s cigarette trade, but the court has not ruled on whether the property purchases were funded by fraud proceeds. The case is continuing in Dubai.

content.headline: Staff shortages leave some Region Zealand ambulances idle for more than a third
content.shortHeadline: Staff shortages leave some Zealand ambulances idle
content.standfirst: Region Zealand says it lacks staff to run all its ambulances, with some stations’ vehicles out of service for more than 10% of the time this year. The region says it is reallocating vehicles to maintain response times but expects full staffing only in 2028.

sources.originalTitle: Her er ambulancen ude af drift hver tredje dag

segments.body: About three ambulances are unavailable each day in Region Zealand because of staffing shortages, the region says. In the first eight months of the year, ambulances operated by the region and Falck were idle for 18,000 hours combined; about 90% of those hours involved the region’s own service. At Hvalsø, its sole ambulance was out of service more than 35% of the time.

The region says its dispatch centre reallocates vehicles and uses extra resources to maintain response times, but at Hvalsø only 62% of calls in the area were reached within 15 minutes, below the region’s 90% target. Officials say recruitment has not filled the gap and full staffing is not expected before 2028.

content.headline: Denmark centralises bridge emergency planning as threat level rises
content.shortHeadline: Denmark centralises bridge emergency plans amid higher threats
content.standfirst: Sund & Bælt will take responsibility for contingency planning for the Little Belt and Great Belt crossings, including how traffic could continue if bridges were put out of action. The agreement does not introduce tolls on the Little Belt bridges.

sources.originalTitle: Vil indsætte færger, hvis store broer saboteres

segments.body: Denmark is bringing contingency planning for the Little Belt and Great Belt bridges under Sund & Bælt, replacing a division of responsibilities between several agencies. The transport ministry says the change reflects the threat environment and aims to maintain links between eastern and western Denmark during a crisis.

Sund & Bælt will examine how traffic, including freight, could be handled if both Little Belt bridges were unavailable. The announcement concerns preparedness planning; it does not say that sabotage has occurred. Ownership of both crossings is being transferred to Sund & Bælt, with no tolls planned for the Little Belt bridges.

content.headline: Police urge parents to check whether children’s e-scooters are illegally tuned
content.shortHeadline: Danish police warn parents over fast, illegally tuned e-scooters
content.standfirst: Police say some children’s scooters can reach 80km/h, far above the legal limit, and are urging parents to check them. Authorities cite hundreds of recorded e-scooter crashes since 2020, including serious injuries and one death.

sources.originalTitle: Politiet advarer forældre om ulovlige el-løbehjul

segments.body: Mid- and West Zealand Police are asking parents to check their children’s electric scooters for illegal modifications. An officer says some can reach speeds of up to 80km/h. The police have circulated guidance through municipalities and schools explaining the rules and parents’ responsibilities.

Since 2020, 692 recorded accidents in Denmark have involved e-scooters; 121 people were seriously injured and one died, according to the Danish Road Directorate. Police and road-safety officials say excessive speed can make it difficult for other road users to judge a scooter’s approach. The police say parents should inspect scooters rather than assume they comply.

content.headline: Man dies in head-on crash north of Aarhus
content.shortHeadline: 24-year-old man killed in crash north of Aarhus
content.standfirst: A van and a car collided on Kaløvej on Friday. Two other people were taken to hospital; police say their initial investigation indicates a head-on collision, and the cause has not been established.

image.caption: Archive image of police at a road collision on Kaløvej north of Aarhus.

sources.originalTitle: 24-årig mand omkommet i alvorligt sammenstød nord for Aarhus
24-årig er omkommet i trafikulykke ved Aarhus

segments.body: A 24-year-old man died after a van and a car collided on Kaløvej north of Aarhus on Friday. He was driving the car; a 30-year-old passenger and another person were taken to hospital. Police say neither of the other two had serious injuries, according to the initial account.
Police say their preliminary investigation suggests the vehicles collided head-on and both left the road. The cause of the crash remains unknown.

perspectives.body: TV 2’s report initially said the 30-year-old passenger was seriously injured and later described him as stable. DR’s later account says the two hospitalised people had no serious injuries.

content.headline: Danish director says Texas denied film support over abortion theme; state denies
content.shortHeadline: Danish director alleges Texas rejected film over abortion theme
content.standfirst: Milad Avaz says his film about Texas abortion restrictions was denied a tax incentive after a lengthy application process. The state says it can reject applications under Texas law and denies no specific claim; the official refusal letter cited by DR does not mention abortion.

image.caption: Director Milad Avaz, who says Texas denied his film a tax incentive because it concerns abortion.

sources.originalTitle: I Texas vil man ikke give penge til dansk instruktørs abortfilm

segments.body: Danish-Iranian director Milad Avaz says Texas authorities withdrew support for his film Elastic Hearts because it concerns abortion. He says a commission contact told the production, “You made a film about abortions in Texas, what did you expect?” The film was shot in Texas and is due for Danish cinema release next year.

segments.title: The reason for the decision is disputed
segments.body: The official refusal letter reviewed by DR does not mention abortion, so the outlet says there is no documentary evidence that this was the reason. Governor Greg Abbott’s spokesperson says Texas may decline grant applications and does not use public money for projects that portray Texas or Texans negatively. The governor did not answer DR’s specific questions.

content.headline: Grealish faces a test of trust after Everton discipline breach
content.shortHeadline: Grealish must rebuild trust after Everton breach
content.standfirst: Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s cup win after missing training, and the club’s public explanation underlined the seriousness of the breach. With options limited, David Moyes will hope the forward can regain the club’s trust.

image.caption: Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for the Newcastle cup tie after a breach of club discipline.

sources.originalTitle: Britain's first £100m man facing defining moment

segments.body: Grealish missed training on Monday and was excluded from Everton’s squad to face Newcastle, with the club describing the matter as a breach of discipline. The 3-1 win sent Everton into the EFL Cup quarter-finals, but the incident has put the forward’s place and his relationship with the club under scrutiny.

segments.title: A chance to make amends
segments.body: BBC Sport reports that Grealish has spoken with club officials and that Everton do not regard this incident as a final warning. But Moyes has a small squad, and Grealish has yet to score or provide an assist in eight appearances this season. He now has to show he can meet the club’s expectations and contribute on the pitch.

content.headline: England beat USA as Red Roses’ rebuilding work continues
content.shortHeadline: England beat USA, but set-piece concerns remain
content.standfirst: England ended their WXV Global Series with a win in New Jersey, led by Claudia Moloney-MacDonald’s four tries. The performance offered positives after two defeats by Canada, but left coach John Mitchell with work to do before the Six Nations.

image.caption: Claudia Moloney-MacDonald scored four tries in England’s win over the United States.

sources.originalTitle: England see off USA to return to winning ways
From her own Barbie doll to bench - how Ellie Kildunne slipped from Red Roses' XV

segments.body: Claudia Moloney-MacDonald scored four tries as England beat the United States to return to winning ways. The hosts stayed in the contest with physical defence and a late try, while England’s scrum and line-out came under pressure. England’s depth and finishing told in the final quarter.

segments.title: Kildunne’s place is not guaranteed
segments.body: Ellie Kildunne came off the bench rather than starting at full-back. BBC Sport’s analysis says coach John Mitchell pointed to a difficult spell and the need for consistency, while Emma Sing’s strong form and different skill set have strengthened the competition for the position.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport’s analysis notes that Kildunne’s recent international statistics have declined and that opponents, including Canada, have found ways to limit her. It presents Sing’s selection as a genuine alternative, not simply a temporary cover.

content.headline: England’s Rugby League World Cup campaign faces a double setback
content.shortHeadline: England’s Rugby League World Cup hopes unravel
content.standfirst: England’s women are out after losing to Samoa, while the men’s win over Papua New Guinea was not enough to put them in control of qualification. The defeats have sharpened questions about preparation, investment and the gap to southern hemisphere teams.

image.caption: England beat Papua New Guinea 34-12, but the margin left their World Cup hopes hanging on another result.

sources.originalTitle: Set up to fail? Where England's World Cup campaign went wrong

segments.body: England’s women lost 24-6 to Samoa and will not reach the semi-finals. The men beat Papua New Guinea 34-12, but needed a much bigger margin to improve their position. Their elimination will be confirmed on Sunday unless Tonga beat Samoa by more than 46 points.

segments.title: Preparation and resources under scrutiny
segments.body: The men’s campaign was hampered by injuries, difficult travel and a short preparation period after head coach Brian McDermott’s appointment in April. England’s women, meanwhile, were beaten by Australia and Samoa; coach Stuart Barrow said the NRLW’s investment is accelerating the game in the Pacific and called for more funding for the women’s game at home.

content.headline: African football restores Afcon’s two-year cycle after U-turn
content.shortHeadline: Afcon stays biennial after Caf reverses course
content.standfirst: The Confederation of African Football has abandoned its plan to stage the Africa Cup of Nations every four years and will keep the tournament on a two-year cycle. The reversal renews debate over the competition’s finances and who should shape its future.

image.caption: Senegal’s Afcon 2025 title was later awarded to Morocco; the Court of Arbitration for Sport will decide the outcome.

sources.originalTitle: Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?

segments.body: Caf president Patrice Motsepe said the tournament would return to its traditional two-year schedule, reversing a decision made last December to move to a four-year cycle from 2028. The governing body also plans to retain the 2028 edition, though its host and exact dates have not yet been announced.

segments.title: A financial and governance question
segments.body: Afcon is a major source of income for Caf and helps fund national-team programmes, while the proposed Africa Nations League is yet to demonstrate that it could replace that support. The original cycle change was approved by Caf’s executive committee without being put to a general assembly, drawing criticism over how the decision was made.

content.headline: Zverev overwhelms Fery in Vienna as Rybakina withdraws in Tokyo
content.shortHeadline: Zverev cruises past Fery; Rybakina withdraws injured
content.standfirst: Alexander Zverev needed 58 minutes to beat Britain’s Arthur Fery and reach the Vienna semi-finals. In Tokyo, Elena Rybakina withdrew from her quarter-final with a neck injury, a day after securing the year-end world number one ranking.

image.caption: Alexander Zverev beat Arthur Fery in straight sets to reach the Vienna semi-finals.

sources.originalTitle: Zverev thrashes GB's Fery to reach Vienna semis

segments.body: Zverev defeated Fery 6-0 6-2, dropping only six points on serve as he reached the last four in Vienna. Fery, who had beaten Lorenzo Musetti to reach the quarter-finals, had received treatment on his leg during that earlier match. Zverev is set to replace Jannik Sinner at the top of the men’s rankings.

Rybakina withdrew from her Tokyo quarter-final against Leylah Fernandez with a neck injury. Fernandez received a walkover. Rybakina had made the year-end women’s number one ranking unassailable the previous day.

content.headline: Leicester beat Bristol to go top before the weekend’s remaining games
content.shortHeadline: Leicester edge Bristol and move top of the Prem
content.standfirst: Leicester took a 22-16 away win over Bristol to move above Gloucester at the summit, ahead of the rest of the weekend’s matches. A late penalty kept the hosts in contention, but the Tigers held on for a bonus-point victory.

image.caption: Ollie Hassell-Collins scored Leicester’s third try against Bristol.

sources.originalTitle: Leicester dominate Bristol to go top of the Prem

segments.body: Tries from Freddie Steward, Adam Radwan, Ollie Hassell-Collins and Jamie Blamire helped Leicester beat Bristol 22-16. Blamire’s try secured the bonus point, while James Williams’ third penalty brought Bristol within six points and set up a tense finish. Leicester held on.

Leicester went top of the Prem before the rest of the weekend’s fixtures, having arrived level with Bristol on three wins apiece. Bristol director of rugby Pat Lam said his side had not applied enough pressure, while Leicester head coach Geoff Parling called it a gritty win after a demanding run of games.

content.headline: Anderson says Lancashire exit left him questioning his future
content.shortHeadline: Anderson shocked by Lancashire exit and unsure what’s next
content.standfirst: James Anderson says he was shocked when Lancashire told him they would not renew his contract, and that the decision made him question himself. The 44-year-old has not decided whether to continue playing for another county.

image.caption: James Anderson is England’s leading Test wicket-taker, with 704 dismissals.

sources.originalTitle: Anderson 'shocked' by Lancs exit and unsure if he will continue

segments.body: Anderson said he went into a meeting expecting to discuss how Lancashire’s team could move forward, only to be told the club wanted to build an attack for the future without him. He took 50 County Championship wickets last season and captained Lancashire, who finished second bottom in Division Two.

segments.title: An undecided next chapter
segments.body: The England record wicket-taker said the news made him wonder whether something was fundamentally wrong with him. He is still processing the decision and has not settled on whether to play for another county, although the report says other counties are interested. Stuart Broad criticised Lancashire’s decision and the absence of a farewell.

content.headline: Robinson’s Hampden record offers Aberdeen hope against Rangers
content.shortHeadline: Can Robinson’s cup record lift Aberdeen against Rangers?
content.standfirst: Aberdeen manager Stephen Robinson arrives at the League Cup semi-final under pressure, but has never lost a semi-final at Hampden. Rangers have a chance to move closer to their first trophy under Derek McInnes, with both clubs facing a high-stakes test.

image.caption: Stephen Robinson has a strong record in cup competitions against Derek McInnes.

sources.originalTitle: Can Robinson work Hampden magic against McInnes' Rangers?

segments.body: Robinson’s Aberdeen have won three of their opening 11 league games and have struggled for goals at home. His record in Hampden semi-finals offers a reason for hope: he has reached this stage with previous clubs and won the League Cup with St Mirren last season.

segments.title: Pressure on both managers
segments.body: Rangers, unbeaten in 10 games, have already beaten Celtic to reach the semi-final and are chasing their first trophy under McInnes. The BBC’s analysis warns that a defeat to a struggling Aberdeen would set Rangers back, while a win could give McInnes an early opportunity to build belief at Ibrox.

content.headline: Skepta says his new album puts conscious messages over a grime pulse
content.shortHeadline: Skepta brings a more conscious voice to his new album
content.standfirst: The grime star says fatherhood and a reckoning with past mistakes shaped The Fork and Knife, his first solo album since 2019. He also discusses immigration, multicultural Britain and the responsibility that comes with his voice.

image.caption: Skepta, whose new album draws on his reflections about music and responsibility.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ignorance towards immigration is horrible. It’s not British’: Skepta on his long-awaited return – and his anger at the racist right

segments.body: Skepta says The Fork and Knife, due next week, took seven years to make because he wanted to be more mindful about what he says. The 15-track album still makes room for grime and party music, but he describes its aim as delivering conscious messages “but still have a vibe”.

segments.title: A British story
segments.body: On “Innocent Smile”, featuring Madness singer Suggs, Skepta draws on his family’s Nigerian heritage and the multicultural life he grew up with in Tottenham. He says his father played ska at home and remembers Black people and skinheads meeting at east London parties. The interview also revisits his apologies for past missteps, including the 2024 album artwork that inadvertently evoked the Holocaust.

content.headline: Bombstrap lead a week of new tracks with Rotterdam’s uncompromising punk
content.shortHeadline: Bombstrap lead this week’s new tracks with Rotterdam punk
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s weekly selection introduces the theatrical noise of Bombstrap, led by vocalist and visual artist Eva Kah, alongside seven new tracks spanning house, jazz, techno-pop and dream pop.

image.caption: Eva Kah of Bombstrap, the Rotterdam band featured in this week’s new-track selection.

sources.originalTitle: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: Dutch squat-punks Bombstrap’s uncompromising racket

segments.body: Rotterdam band Bombstrap draw on hardcore punk, art-school eccentricity and the communal squatting scene around Het Poortgebouw. The Guardian’s feature describes their debut Big Enemy as a shifting, high-volume sound, led by Eva Kah’s confrontational performance and an attitude at odds with the city’s gentrification.

segments.title: More new sounds
segments.body: The playlist moves well beyond punk: Clementine Douglas brings deep vocal house, DJ Heartstring pair breakbeats with spoken-word passages, and saxophonist Josh Johnson sets two melodic motifs against analogue synth. Other picks include bright techno-pop from Isaac Kniveton, shoegaze-leaning Anamanaguchi, Japanese artist Metoronori and a new lullaby from Waterbaby.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut turns traditional songs into startling testimony
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat gives traditional songs startling force
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer’s first solo album gathers songs of women’s suffering and endurance, from a battered wife’s divided loyalties to a lament for Ireland. The review praises its spare arrangements and visceral performances.

image.caption: Radie Peat, whose solo debut reworks traditional songs of struggle and endurance.

sources.originalTitle: Radie Peat: No Human Tongue Can Tell review – Lankum singer’s solo debut is the year’s best folk album

segments.body: On No Human Tongue Can Tell, Radie Peat begins with a stark voice and subtle piano before adding layers of Mellotron and Wurlitzer. The review finds a unifying theme of female struggle, strength and endurance in a collection that draws much of its power from songs Peat has performed for years.

segments.title: Songs that carry their history
segments.body: Peat gives “Willow Garden” the weight of a haunting elegy, while “Still I Love Him” holds the tension of a woman emotionally bound to the husband who beats her. “Dark Horse on the Wind”, Liam Weldon’s lament for the lost dream of the Irish republic, ends the review’s examples on a stark note. Producer John “Spud” Murphy’s textures bring out the detail of Peat’s concertina and Eleanor Myler’s drums.

content.headline: Kali Malone finds a more direct, emotionally charged sound on Burning Song
content.shortHeadline: Kali Malone turns toward emotion on Burning Song
content.standfirst: The US drone composer takes a more compact approach on her new album, recorded on the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche. The review hears a sombre, carefully controlled shift toward direct feeling.

image.caption: Kali Malone, whose new album uses the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche.

sources.originalTitle: Kali Malone: Burning Song review – drone composer wields Bach’s organ to breathtaking effect

segments.body: Burning Song is unusually compact by Kali Malone’s standards: its pieces are shorter than the extended works that established her reputation, and it sets aside the contrapuntal canon form. Malone plays the Bach organ at Leipzig’s Thomaskirche with cellist Lucy Railton and bowed-guitar player Stephen O’Malley.

segments.title: Attention in the details
segments.body: The review describes the trio’s sound as a close interplay of crackle, breath and scrape. “Grieving Figure” moves from a distant, sustained note toward a brighter finish, while “Bells on a Branch” ends in a dry, depleted mood. The album’s emotional directness, the critic argues, remains restrained rather than reaching for easy grandeur.

content.headline: CDs find new listeners as fans look for music beyond streaming
content.shortHeadline: Why CDs are finding listeners again
content.standfirst: Searches for CD players at John Lewis are up 96% since July, while a separate report found CD sales up 16%. Music fans explain what physical discs offer that streaming does not: ownership, focus and a more deliberate way to listen.

image.caption: Young people choosing CDs in a music shop in Munich.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback

segments.body: The Guardian reports rising interest in CDs, drawing on figures from John Lewis and a music-and-film trends report. The fans it spoke to describe different reasons for returning to the format: some never left it, while others have turned to discs after finding vinyl bulky or streaming’s endless choices overwhelming.

segments.title: A more deliberate listen
segments.body: Several interviewees value owning music that might disappear from streaming services, and one buys directly from independent and folk musicians so they receive a larger share of the money. Others say a CD encourages attention to an album as a whole, without autoplay or algorithmic playlists. Not everyone rejects streaming: one collector uses it to discover music before buying discs.

content.headline: Satanic Planet’s Dead Deities makes provocation part of its noisy craft
content.shortHeadline: Satanic Planet make a noisy, provocative album
content.standfirst: The metal group led by Satanic Temple co-founder Lucien Greaves pairs political provocation with industrial noise, choral organs and precise, heavy arrangements. The review finds a compelling record, though not every lyric escapes its own edginess.

sources.originalTitle: Dead Deities

segments.body: Satanic Planet is a metal supergroup featuring producer Luke Henshaw, the Locust’s Justin Pearson and drummer Dave Lombardo. On Dead Deities, the band’s second album, Lucien Greaves brings the project’s political intent to music that moves between experimental metal, industrial textures and processed vocals.

segments.title: More than a provocation
segments.body: The review singles out the heavy organ and noisy textures of “Church Burning” and the tension-building arrangement of “Ouroboros”. It praises the group’s attention to sound as a reason the album avoids slipping into parody, while also calling the lyrics of “Sam Alito’s Mom” arguably misogynistic and questioning how fresh some of the record’s anti-authoritarian slogans feel.

content.headline: Olivia Tremor Control’s final album turns mortality into psychedelic pop
content.shortHeadline: Olivia Tremor Control’s final album faces mortality
content.standfirst: The Elephant 6 band’s first album in 27 years arrives after the deaths of founding members Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart. Its familiar pop and sound collages now carry an unsettling weight, the review argues.

sources.originalTitle: The Same Place

segments.body: The Same Place, the Olivia Tremor Control’s third and final album, has been in progress since 2010. Most of it was recorded between 2010 and 2012; other members and collaborators added finishing touches after co-frontmen Bill Doss and Will Cullen Hart died.

segments.title: A familiar sound, newly shadowed
segments.body: The review hears the band’s characteristic pop instincts and sound-collage experiments, but with a persistent darkness around them. Songs that circle time and mortality—including the winding “The Spinning Continuous”—make the album feel newly poignant, without resolving the questions it raises. The result is both a return to a beloved band and a postscript to the Elephant 6 scene.

content.headline: Mackeeper turn aughts pop nostalgia into sly, finely made songs
content.shortHeadline: Mackeeper’s debut makes a game of pop nostalgia
content.standfirst: The New York duo’s first full-length reaches back to the pop-rock swagger of the 2000s, from guitar solos to boy-band melodies. The review finds that their teasing, self-aware approach is matched by serious craft.

sources.originalTitle: Believe You Me

segments.body: Mackeeper’s debut album, Believe You Me, draws on the duo’s upbringing with Top 40 music and music-production software. The review hears echoes of early-2000s pop, rap-rock and grunge, assembled into songs that are carefully arranged even when Cohen and Harwood play at being scraggly anti-heroes.

segments.title: The joke and the song
segments.body: Miles Cohen’s vocal shifts from boyish earnestness to a more forceful snarl, while “Men in Black” combines crunchy guitars, half-time drums and playful ad-libs. The critic’s central pleasure is the tension between the duo’s wink at pop conventions and their obvious skill at making hooks that work on their own terms.

content.headline: Kentridge’s Shostakovich animation finds black comedy in Soviet history
content.shortHeadline: Kentridge turns Shostakovich into a comic, dark ballet
content.standfirst: Oh to Believe in Another World pairs a collage animation and live choreography with Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony. The review sees the work’s humour as part of its response to Stalinist tyranny and the loss of revolutionary idealism.

image.caption: An image from William Kentridge’s Oh to Believe in Another World.

sources.originalTitle: Oh to Believe in Another World review – William Kentridge’s amazing animated ballet of black comic pain

segments.body: William Kentridge’s hour-long cine-musical uses masks, models, dancers and live-action choreography to accompany Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony. Its Soviet figures—including Stalin, Lenin, Trotsky and poet Vladimir Mayakovsky—move through meticulously built miniature settings that become, through the film’s effects, almost lifesize.

segments.title: A laugh with a shadow
segments.body: The review is struck by the work’s black comedy: Stalin’s monumental face remains fixed while the dancer beneath it capers. That humour sits alongside photographs of people targeted by the state and the symphony’s ambiguous mix of fear, revulsion and grief. For the critic, the film is shaped for the music, and its longing for another world mourns both lost idealism and what replaced it.

content.headline: Ten films beyond horror that can still leave viewers frightened
content.shortHeadline: Ten terrifying films that aren’t horror
content.standfirst: Guardian writers pick films that unsettle through human cruelty, social dread and the unknown rather than relying on the conventions of horror. Their choices range from The Hunchback of Notre Dame to 2001: A Space Odyssey.

image.caption: Mia McKenna-Bruce in How to Have Sex, one of the films in the selection.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror movies

segments.body: The selection looks beyond the horror genre for films that frighten by other means. Its choices include the creeping menace of Lee Chang-dong’s Burning, the cruelty and bigotry in Disney’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame, and the dread of a young girl’s holiday in How to Have Sex.

segments.title: Dread in different forms
segments.body: Other writers point to 2001: A Space Odyssey’s fear of human technology, the grim investigation in The Sniper and the oppressive atmosphere of Dark Waters. The recommendations also include the anxiety of The Hunt, Zodiac and Requiem for a Dream, showing how suspense, injustice and human behaviour can unsettle as powerfully as monsters or jump scares.

content.headline: Wicker makes a strange romantic fantasy from a woman’s wish for kindness
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s odd romance has a serious argument beneath it
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of wicker, played by Alexander Skarsgård. An interview and a sharply dissenting review see the comic fantasy as both a challenge to convention and an uneasy story about his lack of agency.

image.caption: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie Wicker
Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a fisherwoman mocked by her village asks a basketmaker to make her a husband. The result is Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband, a creature devoted to her happiness. Colman and the film-makers describe the story as an earthy, bawdy fairy tale in which a woman who has little place in the village’s conventions gets to choose the shape of her own life.

segments.title: Fantasy and its limits
segments.body: The i Paper’s review enjoys the film’s comic, horny absurdity but argues that the Wicker Husband’s own wishes receive too little attention: his devotion is not the same as free choice. The Guardian interview emphasises the Fisherwoman’s agency and the film’s satire of patriarchal marriage. Together, the accounts capture the tension between the film’s playful wish-fulfilment and its questions about equality.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s critic argues that the film’s central joke has a troubling edge: the Wicker Husband is expected to serve his wife and accept danger, with little attention paid to his own desires.

content.headline: The Mosquito Bowl mixes football and war but leans on familiar heroics
content.shortHeadline: The Mosquito Bowl pairs war action with stale heroics
content.standfirst: Peter Berg’s Second World War drama links a football game among US marines with the battle of Okinawa. The review praises its absorbing action while questioning its clichés and the way Japanese suffering sits at the edge of the story.

image.caption: Nicholas Galitzine and Ray Nicholson in The Mosquito Bowl.

sources.originalTitle: The Mosquito Bowl review – Netflix mixes football, war and cliches in slick by-the-numbers saga

segments.body: The Mosquito Bowl follows college football players who joined the US marines after Pearl Harbor and a 1944 game on Guadalcanal. The review finds the action sequences effective, with the movement and camaraderie of sport giving the film a visual way to connect the football field with the battlefield.

segments.title: Whose war is shown?
segments.body: The critic finds the dialogue heavy with familiar speeches about honour and duty, and questions how the film balances period-accurate racism among US soldiers with its own point of view. Its emphasis on American suffering, the review argues, sits uneasily beside the largely unnamed anguish of Japanese soldiers and civilians at Okinawa.

content.headline: Elke Sommer, star of A Shot in the Dark, dies aged 85
content.shortHeadline: Elke Sommer, star of A Shot in the Dark, dies aged 85
content.standfirst: The German-born actor appeared in Hollywood films with Peter Sellers, Paul Newman and Dick Van Dyke, as well as British comedies and horror films. Bild magazine reported that she died in Los Angeles of heart failure.

image.caption: Elke Sommer, the German-born actor whose career spanned European and Hollywood films.

sources.originalTitle: Elke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85

segments.body: Elke Sommer, whose roles included the maid suspected of murder in the Pink Panther sequel A Shot in the Dark, has died aged 85. Bild magazine reported that she died in Los Angeles of heart failure. Born Elke Schletz in Berlin, she was evacuated to Bavaria during the war and was spotted by Vittorio De Sica after winning a beauty contest in Italy.

segments.title: A career across languages
segments.body: Sommer’s gift for languages helped her move between Italian, German, British and Hollywood films. Her credits included The Prize with Paul Newman, And Then There Were None and Carry on Behind. In the 1970s she also appeared in two horror films by Mario Bava, before later concentrating on painting.

content.headline: Gentle Monster examines the loyalty that keeps women close to troubled men
content.shortHeadline: Gentle Monster asks what loyalty costs two women
content.standfirst: Marie Kreutzer’s drama follows a musician whose husband is under police investigation and a detective who makes excuses for her father. Its central tension lies in what remains unknown about the men they love.

image.caption: Léa Seydoux in Gentle Monster.

sources.originalTitle: Gentle Monster review – disquieting drama about two women facing the truth about the men they love

segments.body: Lucy Weiss, a French musician played by Léa Seydoux, has moved to the countryside to support her husband after his breakdown. Then detective Elsa arrives with a search warrant and removes his devices. The film follows Lucy’s struggle to understand what he has done, while Elsa pursues a case and avoids confronting her own father’s behaviour.

segments.title: The pain of not knowing
segments.body: The police find no evidence that Lucy’s son has been abused, but Elsa warns that certainty is impossible. Lucy, meanwhile, hears shifting explanations from her husband and tries to make them fit what she sees. The review calls this a bleak drama about loyalty and denial, anchored by Seydoux and Jella Haase’s contrasting performances.

content.headline: Twelve family-friendly films for a Halloween night with scares
content.shortHeadline: Twelve spooky films to watch with the family
content.standfirst: This Halloween guide offers a dozen films that aim to frighten without resorting to the most extreme horror. It ranges from Coraline and Goosebumps to The Others and Poltergeist, with a reminder to check the age ratings.

image.caption: A Halloween guide to scary films for family viewing.

sources.originalTitle: 12 scary films you can actually watch with your kids this Halloween

segments.body: The guide suggests films for families seeking a Halloween scare, while noting that parental discretion matters. Its choices include Coraline’s unsettling stop-motion fantasy, the comic creature chaos of Gremlins and the ghost story The Others, which finds its unease in atmosphere rather than explicit violence.

segments.title: For older viewers
segments.body: Other picks include The Woman in Black, The Sixth Sense and Poltergeist. The guide flags Crimson Peak as more suitable for older teens because of its bloody imagery and adult themes, and provides age-rating context to help families choose what fits their children.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning draws sharply different verdicts on Facebook’s harms
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning: chilling exposé or toothless drama?
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s film dramatises the Facebook Files, journalist Jeff Horwitz’s reporting on the company’s platform. One review finds an unsettling warning about social media’s hold on daily life; another says the drama lacks urgency and is unlikely to change minds.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows journalist Jeff Horwitz and whistleblower Frances Haugen as they uncover Facebook research and decisions tied to users’ wellbeing and political misinformation. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg. The i Paper review says the film’s dark tone turns the investigation into a story about a system viewers are already part of.

segments.title: Two readings of its impact
segments.body: The i Paper writer finds the film frightening partly because the real-life revelations have become so familiar that people can grow numb to them. The BBC’s review reaches a less favourable verdict: it praises the opening and some of the reporting, but finds little tension, a limited Zuckerberg character and no real reckoning. The disagreement is over whether the film makes a compelling warning or an ineffective drama.

perspectives.body: The BBC critic argues that the film’s investigative premise never becomes a tense drama: Horwitz and Haugen are not threatened, and the story’s strands do not meaningfully converge.

content.headline: SCTV’s oddball sketch comedy gave a generation of stars its start
content.shortHeadline: How SCTV made room for comedy that refused to dumb down
content.standfirst: Dave Thomas recalls the Canadian sketch show that launched John Candy, Eugene Levy and Catherine O’Hara, and influenced The Simpsons. A new documentary and the release of 134 episodes bring its layered, low-budget comedy back into view.

image.caption: Members of SCTV’s cast, including Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and Eugene Levy.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It really was the idiots in charge’: inside the TV sketch show that launched a generation of stars

segments.body: Second City Television followed a run-down station in the fictional Canadian town of Melonville, making its limited budget part of the joke. Dave Thomas, an original cast member and head writer, says the show aimed high with its references and trusted viewers to keep up. Its cast also included John Candy, Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, Rick Moranis and Andrea Martin.

segments.title: Making the constraints work
segments.body: Thomas says the early show was a failure, but its makeshift look gave the writers room to build distinctive characters and interlocking parodies. The approach later influenced The Simpsons, whose writers admired SCTV’s layered comedy. Thomas is less impressed by the new documentary’s omissions, including its limited attention to the show’s writers and musical guests.

content.headline: Awkwafina returns to her family’s restaurant story in a personal cooking series
content.shortHeadline: Awkwafina explores family history through food
content.standfirst: In Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, Nora Lum travels across the US to learn from Asian American chefs and consider whether her family restaurant can return. She talks about the show’s connection to her late grandmother and the restaurant’s place in her family history.

image.caption: Awkwafina, also known as Nora Lum, whose series follows her family’s restaurant history.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandma

segments.body: Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook follows Nora Lum as she learns from a new generation of Asian American chefs, with the hope of reviving her family’s long-closed Cantonese restaurant. Lum says the restaurant, opened by her great-grandfather in Flushing, Queens, helped bring the family to the US and remained a presence in family life after it closed in 1982.

segments.title: A family story on screen
segments.body: Lum describes the series as a love letter to her grandmother, who helped raise her after her mother died. She also reflects on the work and sacrifices behind restaurant life, including the family’s losses when her grandmother’s business failed. The show’s warm approach, she says, does not set out to make a political point, but immigrant experience is inseparable from the story of Chinese-American food.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ biggest turns—and the debate over James Acaster
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors: its best moments and Acaster’s exit
content.standfirst: A highlights roundup revisits the celebrity series’ mistakes, reversals and one-liners. A second account argues that James Acaster’s decision to confess as a Traitor drained the game of the tension viewers wanted.

image.caption: A moment from The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Game-breaking blunders, killer yawns … and a puddle of vomit: it’s the top 10 Celebrity Traitors moments
James Acaster has made a mockery of The Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The Guardian’s countdown recalls the camp opening, Ross Kemp’s spiralling paranoia, Jerry Hall’s one-liners and the surprise of three Traitors receiving a special power. It also tracks the game’s volatile alliances and Acaster’s unusual decision to play against the role he had been given.

segments.title: A confession that split opinion
segments.body: The i Paper’s critic was frustrated when Acaster admitted he had been recruited as a Traitor and was “a Faithful at heart”. The piece argues that his confession cut short a tense confrontation and let the other players avoid fully testing their suspicions of Maya Jama. It reflects a different expectation of the format from the broader highlights roundup.

perspectives.body: The i Paper critic says Acaster’s early confession robbed the episode of a proper contest, arguing that players and viewers invest in seeing the Traitors pushed to defend themselves.

content.headline: Matthew Perry’s own memoir makes Netflix’s new documentary feel intrusive
content.shortHeadline: A Matthew Perry documentary revisits what he already told us
content.standfirst: The One About Matthew Perry draws on interviews with his family and archive footage, but the review argues that its retelling adds little to his own memoir. It finds the treatment of his death both cursory and painful for those close to him.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The three-part documentary follows Perry from aspiring actor to Friends star and addiction campaigner, using archive footage and accounts from people close to him. The review finds parts of it moving, but notes that Perry had already described his addiction in detail in his 2022 memoir, Friends, Lovers and the Big Terrible Thing.

segments.title: What the documentary leaves out
segments.body: The critic says the film moves quickly past unresolved questions about Perry’s death and the people who supplied him with ketamine, instead lingering on relatives’ recollections of learning that he had died. The review questions whether that access serves viewers or Perry’s memory, while acknowledging the emotion of seeing his Friends castmates attend his funeral together.

content.headline: Call the Midwife’s Laura Main reflects on the show’s break and caring for her 91
content.shortHeadline: Laura Main on Call the Midwife, caring and a new role
content.standfirst: After 15 years on Call the Midwife, Laura Main is spending the show’s hiatus on stage and helping care for her mother. She discusses playing the Queen’s dresser and why she wanted Shelagh to age naturally.

image.caption: Laura Main, who plays the Queen’s dresser in By Royal Appointment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I wanted my Call the Midwife character to age normally – even if I didn’t want to’

segments.body: Laura Main has not filmed Call the Midwife this year, as the BBC drama takes a break and prepares a prequel, Sisters in Arms. Main says she will miss the programme, where she has played Shelagh since 2012, but the pause has also allowed her to help care for her 91-year-old mother in Aberdeen.

segments.title: A different part to play
segments.body: Main is touring in By Royal Appointment, a play about Elizabeth II in which she plays the Queen’s dresser and confidant. She says she felt strongly that Shelagh should age at the character’s natural rate, even if she might prefer otherwise. She also describes the practical support her family received from Aberdeen council and worries that many carers have to leave paid work.

content.headline: After decades playing games, GamesMaster’s Dominik Diamond becomes one
content.shortHeadline: GamesMaster’s Dominik Diamond steps inside a game
content.standfirst: The broadcaster voices the hero of the indie survival horror game Black Tides: Draga’s Wake. He describes the strangeness of hearing himself in the role—and the moment his children realised their father was on screen.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist voiced by Dominik Diamond in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: After 50 years of playing video games, Dominik Diamond has taken a voice role in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake. The game is a survival horror story set aboard a decaying steamship after a heist goes wrong; Diamond voices Draga, a sailor infected by an ancient god.

segments.title: A personal performance
segments.body: Diamond says he initially disliked hearing his voice against the game’s powerful-looking hero, but found a quieter delivery that suited the character. Recording improvised fight sounds felt especially strange. His favourite moment came when he played clips to his children without telling them he was involved, then watched them recognise their father.

content.headline: Lara Croft at 30: the missteps behind gaming’s enduring icon
content.shortHeadline: Lara Croft at 30: the failures that couldn’t undo her
content.standfirst: The Tomb Raider anniversary prompts a look at the character’s worst games, awkward advertising and recurring attempts to recast her as a damsel. The feature argues that Lara’s appeal survived repeated failures to understand what made her compelling.

image.caption: Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV–VI Remastered.

sources.originalTitle: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

segments.body: Thirty years after Lara Croft’s debut, the feature looks beyond the series’ successes to its less celebrated decisions. It revisits the annual release schedule that wore down the original developers, the poorly received Tomb Raider: Chronicles and Angel of Darkness, and marketing that turned Lara into a product as much as a game character.

segments.title: The character beyond the image
segments.body: The article also criticises later games for giving Lara unnecessary sidekicks and for centring her vulnerability and sexualisation. It points to the 2013 reboot’s controversy over a trailer depicting an attempted assault, arguing that such choices missed the appeal of a capable, enigmatic solo adventurer. Despite them, Lara remains a major figure in games culture, with another adventure due next year.

content.headline: Pompeii wardrobe reveals jewellery, cosmetics and a child’s charm necklace
content.shortHeadline: Pompeii wardrobe yields a child’s necklace and daily treasures
content.standfirst: A cabinet sealed by the AD79 eruption held coins, cosmetics and a necklace traditionally worn by children. The finds offer a glimpse of household life in the ancient city—and suggest its occupants may have fled suddenly.

image.caption: Personal belongings uncovered in a Pompeii home on Via dell’Abbondanza.

sources.originalTitle: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

segments.body: Archaeologists have found personal belongings—including tweezers, a perfume bottle, an incense burner and 38 bronze coins—in a wooden wardrobe in a Pompeii home. The cabinet was sealed when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD79; the house stands on Via dell’Abbondanza, one of the city’s busiest streets.

segments.title: A child’s keepsake
segments.body: The most distinctive object is a necklace with more than 20 charms, including figures of the gods Bes and Mercury. Known as a crepundia, this kind of necklace was traditionally worn by children; its charms could rattle to help parents keep track of them and might also help identify a child.

Coins and personal objects left behind may mean the household had to escape at short notice, Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of Pompeii archaeological park, said. Cooking pots and a box with lead weights also suggest someone in the home was a tradesperson; the discovery is part of a wider restoration project.

content.headline: Seabird ‘jet lag’ can send inexperienced shearwaters hundreds of miles off track
content.shortHeadline: Seabird jet lag may send young shearwaters far off course
content.standfirst: Twenty years of tracking data suggest Manx shearwaters can lose their bearings when rapid eastward flights put their body clocks out of sync with local time. Adults corrected small errors; first-time foragers may struggle more.

image.caption: A Manx shearwater, a seabird that navigates using the sun.

sources.originalTitle: Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

segments.body: Manx shearwaters returning to colonies off the west coast of the UK can be thrown off course after flying rapidly east across the Atlantic, a study of 20 years of GPS tracking data suggests. The change in local time can leave the birds’ internal clocks up to about an hour behind, disrupting their use of the sun to navigate.

segments.title: Experience matters
segments.body: Adult birds corrected their bearings in flight. Their errors added an estimated 5km to a 1,000km journey, according to the research. First-time foragers lack the same map sense to reorient themselves and could deviate by hundreds of kilometres, the researchers said.

The findings, published in Science, support the idea that the birds rely heavily on the sun as a compass: errors remained even when they followed coastlines, where landmarks might have helped. Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved, called the finding significant, while noting that the consequences for birds that return to their colonies remain unclear.

content.headline: Venice lagoon was once dry land as sea levels reshaped the Adriatic
content.shortHeadline: Rising seas turned land around Venice into a lagoon
content.standfirst: Seismic data and sediment cores show that the present-day lagoon once extended more than 30 miles inland. Researchers say rising seas also transformed hills and wetlands across the northern Adriatic over thousands of years.

sources.originalTitle: How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon

segments.body: The land where Venice now stands was once dry ground many miles from the coast, according to a reconstruction of the northern Adriatic landscape over the past 10,000 years. Researchers combined seismic data with sediment cores from coastal basins in northern Italy, Slovenia and northern Croatia.

The study, published in Quaternary Science Reviews, indicates the present-day Venice lagoon once stretched more than 30 miles inland. Trieste, now a coastal city, was previously an area of hills overlooking swamps and lagoons.

Sea levels rose in fits and starts, at times by as much as 25mm a year. The changing coastline would have forced Mesolithic hunter-gatherers to adapt their hunting and fishing; a more stable period over the past 6,000 years helped settlements and farming take root.

content.headline: ‘Ferritin face’ symptoms may suggest low iron—but cannot diagnose it
content.shortHeadline: Can your face reveal low iron? Experts say a blood test is needed
content.standfirst: Pallor, dark circles and hair loss can have many causes, although low iron stores may contribute. Experts caution against treating social-media symptom lists as a diagnosis and advise checking levels with a blood test.

image.caption: A blood test can measure ferritin, a protein that stores iron.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?

segments.body: Social media posts use “ferritin face” to describe pallor, dark circles, dry skin and hair loss as signs of low iron.
